items.title: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth would be -18°C on average
items.claim: Earth absorbs sunlight at visible wavelengths and re-emits energy as infrared. Greenhouse gases (water vapour, CO2, methane) absorb infrared on its way out and re-radiate it in all directions — including back to the surface. Without this effect Earth's mean surface temperature would be about -18°C; with it, the actual mean is about 15°C.
items.prompt: Why does an atmospheric trace gas matter so much?

options.text: Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to visible light (which reaches the surface) but opaque to thermal infrared (which the surface emits) — this asymmetry traps energy in the lower atmosphere

items.reveal_title: Asymmetric absorption of visible vs infrared
items.reveal:
Sunlight peaks in the visible (about 500 nm). Earth's surface, at about 288 K, emits in the mid-infrared (peaking around 10 μm). Greenhouse gases (H2O, CO2, CH4, N2O, O3) have vibration modes that resonate with mid-IR but not visible light.

The consequence: sunlight gets in easily; the re-emitted infrared is partly absorbed and re-radiated back down. The lower atmosphere warms.

Pre-industrial CO2: about 280 ppm. Current (2024): about 425 ppm. The added CO2 doesn't dominate by mass — water vapour is far more abundant — but it's a knob humans can turn. Every doubling of CO2 raises equilibrium temperature by an estimated 2.5-4°C (climate sensitivity), with feedbacks (water vapour, ice albedo, clouds) accounting for most of the response.

Without any greenhouse effect at all, Earth would have a mean surface temperature similar to the Moon's: -18°C, with seas frozen solid.
items.why: The greenhouse effect is taught as 'CO2 bad'. The mechanism (selective infrared absorption) is what makes it both an essential planetary process and a climate-change concern.

items.title: An MRI scanner uses a 1.5 tesla magnetic field — 30,000 times Earth's
items.claim: A typical clinical MRI scanner has a magnetic field around 1.5 T; high-field research machines reach 7 T. Generating such a field continuously requires kilometres of niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium to about 4 K, where it becomes superconducting and carries current with no losses.
items.prompt: Why are superconducting magnets used instead of ordinary electromagnets?

options.text: An ordinary copper-wire electromagnet generating 1.5 T over the bore needed for a patient would dissipate megawatts of heat — practical only for brief pulses; a superconducting magnet, once energised, carries the same current forever with essentially no power input
Superconductors produce stronger fields per amp
Liquid helium is required for the radio detection

items.reveal:
A superconducting magnet is energised once (the current is ramped up from zero) and the current loop is closed via a superconducting switch. The current then flows indefinitely with no resistive losses. The magnet maintains its field as long as the helium keeps the wire below its critical temperature.

Liquid helium boils away slowly. A clinical MRI typically uses a 'cold head' refrigerator to recondense escaping helium — losses are then near zero for years. A 'quench' (loss of superconductivity, often from a tiny warm spot) dumps the magnet's stored energy as heat in seconds, boiling the helium and venting it through emergency pipes.

MRI uses the magnetic field to align protons in the patient's tissue; radio-frequency pulses tip the alignment; relaxation back to the field emits signals that are spatially reconstructed into images.
items.why: Superconductivity is taught as a cryogenic curiosity. It is the technology that makes medical MRI imaging possible — and many particle accelerators.

items.title: A bridge tore itself apart from a steady wind
items.claim: On 7 November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State collapsed after four months in service. A wind of about 19 m/s set the deck twisting at its torsional natural frequency. Within hours, the oscillation built up to several metres of amplitude and the structure failed.
items.prompt: How can a steady wind cause unbounded oscillation?

options.text: The wind happened to gust at exactly the right frequency
Aeroelastic flutter — the bridge's torsional motion changed the air flow in a way that fed energy back into the same motion at the same frequency, amplifying every cycle
The wind was much stronger than reported

items.reveal:
Driven resonance: a periodic external force at the natural frequency drives the oscillation higher each cycle. The amplitude grows linearly with time (limited by damping).

Aeroelastic flutter is different and more dangerous: the structure's own motion alters the airflow, which then drives the motion at the same frequency. It's a feedback loop where the driving frequency automatically locks to the response frequency. A steady wind suffices.

The Tacoma Narrows deck was an aerodynamically simple H-shape with a high aspect ratio. It was particularly vulnerable to torsional flutter at moderate wind speeds.

London's Millennium Bridge in 2000 had a similar story but with pedestrians instead of wind. Walkers' lateral footfalls synchronised with the bridge's natural side-to-side mode; the crowd unconsciously walked in step and amplified the swaying. The bridge was closed and dampers fitted.
items.why: Resonance is taught as benign (musical instruments). Aeroelastic flutter is its destructive cousin — and engineers must design against it explicitly.
